sources.title: Student Loan Arrest Warrants and Airport Enforcement
sources.summary: Dave Ananth discusses why overseas borrowers with longstanding student-loan arrears should establish their position before travelling to New Zealand.
sources.text: In this discussion Unresolved New Zealand student-loan arrears can have serious consequences for an overseas-based borrower when Inland Revenue has obtained a court-issued arrest warrant. In this extract from Notes From The Executive, hosted by Mina Amso, Dave Ananth discusses airport enforcement and why a borrower should understand their position before making travel plans. Border intervention is uncommon, but it is real. A borrower may only become aware of a warrant when attempting to leave New Zealand. That possibility needs careful explanation: it does not mean that every overdue student loan creates an arrest risk, and it does not mean that ordinary tax debt automatically results in airport arrest. The student-loan enforcement framework and the circumstances of the individual matter are important. The practical starting point is to establish the loan history, any correspondence from Inland Revenue, and whether enforcement action has been taken. Someone who has been out of contact with IRD for years may not have a complete picture of their obligations. Obtaining advice before travelling allows those uncertainties to be considered, without assuming that a conversation or proposed payment will remove an existing warrant. Dave is a tax barrister and Partner at Meridian Partners specialising in overseas student-loan matters. His work includes student loans, tax disputes and negotiations with Inland Revenue. Advice and any formal engagement depend on the facts. Inland Revenue and the courts retain their statutory powers, and no adviser can guarantee border safety, a particular outcome or a resolution timeframe. Practical points Distinguish student-loan warrant enforcement from ordinary tax debt. Establish the loan and correspondence history before travel. Do not assume every overdue borrower faces arrest. Seek individual advice; a proposed arrangement is not a guarantee about travel. Podcast material: Notes From The Executive, hosted by Mina Amso. Featuring Dave Ananth. sources.title: Three News: Student Loan Reform and Overseas Borrowers
sources.summary: Dave Ananth appeared on Three News on 30 August 2026 to discuss proposed student-loan reforms and the treatment of overseas-based borrowers.
sources.text: Broadcast summary Three News reported on proposed changes to New Zealand’s Student Loan Scheme in its broadcast on 30 August 2026. The report examined proposals intended to encourage graduates to remain in New Zealand while taking a stricter approach to overseas defaults. Dave Ananth appeared as a tax barrister and Partner at Meridian Partners specialising in overseas student-loan matters. Dave acknowledged that student loans are taxpayer-funded obligations that must ultimately be addressed. His concern was about how a repayment policy works in practice. Simply increasing penalties may drive borrowers who have already disengaged further away from Inland Revenue, rather than encouraging renewed contact, repayment and compliance. The discussion placed that concern within the wider public debate about the proposed reforms. This was independent national media coverage of Dave’s student-loan policy analysis. It was not an advertisement, a prediction about an individual borrower’s matter or an announcement that any particular proposal had become law. Borrowers should distinguish the policy discussion in the broadcast from the rules applying to their own circumstances and from any current IRD decision. The embedded player is provided by Three News through Brightcove; the footage is not hosted by DaveTaxNZ. The relevant segment begins at approximately 0:43 and concludes at approximately 4:09. sources.title: When Discussions With Inland Revenue Go Nowhere
sources.summary: Dave Ananth explains the practical role of professional intervention when communication with Inland Revenue has not resolved a tax matter.
sources.text: In this discussion People often seek legal assistance after they or their advisers have already spoken with Inland Revenue without reaching a workable resolution. In this extract from Notes From The Executive, hosted by Mina Amso, Dave Ananth describes the pressure that can build when a tax problem remains unresolved despite those conversations. The difficulty may extend beyond the tax balance. A business may be struggling to meet commitments while its owner also faces mortgage payments, family difficulties and considerable personal stress. Repeating the same conversation without a clear account of the facts can leave everyone uncertain about what should happen next. Professional involvement starts with understanding that position rather than assuming a particular concession is available. A useful assessment brings together the correspondence, the stage the matter has reached and the financial information needed to evaluate practical options. Clear communication with IRD may include a request for sufficient time to understand the position and prepare a considered response. The purpose is to give an already difficult situation some structure and prevent important issues from being lost in a rushed exchange. Dave is a Partner at Meridian Partners whose work includes student loans, tax disputes and negotiations with Inland Revenue. Legal and accounting input may serve different, complementary roles. Inland Revenue decides whether to allow additional time or accept a proposal. The clip does not promise a pause in enforcement, a reduction in debt or an agreed arrangement. Individual advice requires conflict and engagement checks before detailed confidential information is provided. Practical points Bring together previous IRD correspondence and unresolved questions. Identify the current stage of the matter and any approaching deadlines. Work with the accountant to establish reliable financial information. Treat requests for time or an arrangement as proposals, not guaranteed outcomes. Podcast material: Notes From The Executive, hosted by Mina Amso. Featuring Dave Ananth. sources.title: PAYE Arrears and Potential Criminal Liability
sources.summary: PAYE arrears require early attention. Dave Ananth discusses employer deductions and the potential consequences of persistent non-compliance.
sources.text: In this discussion PAYE deducted from employees’ wages is not ordinary business working capital. In this Notes From The Executive extract, hosted by Mina Amso, Dave Ananth explains why employer deductions need particular attention when a business is under financial pressure. Using those deductions to meet other expenses does not remove the obligation to account for them to Inland Revenue. Persistent failure to account for employer deductions can expose business owners and directors to serious enforcement and, in appropriate cases, prosecution. Criminal liability depends on the applicable law and the circumstances; the existence of arrears alone should not be presented as a conclusion that a particular person has committed an offence. Inland Revenue and the courts have their own decision-making responsibilities. The practical lesson is to identify payment difficulties early. Directors should speak with their accountant and lawyer before unpaid PAYE becomes part of a larger pattern of non-compliance. An accurate picture of deductions, amounts paid, outstanding returns and previous IRD correspondence helps those advisers understand what needs attention. A business should not assume that continuing to trade will, by itself, solve an accumulating shortfall. Dave’s commentary focuses on recognising the seriousness of the position and obtaining appropriate advice. It is not a promise that prosecution can be prevented or that Inland Revenue will accept a payment proposal. Meridian Partners can discuss whether a matter falls within the relevant practice and what the next steps may be. Initial contact should remain brief until conflicts have been checked and a formal engagement is agreed. Practical points Keep employer deductions distinct from available working capital. Identify missed PAYE payments and outstanding obligations promptly. Involve the accountant and lawyer before a pattern of non-compliance develops. Do not assume arrears establish criminal liability or that advice guarantees protection. Podcast material: Notes From The Executive, hosted by Mina Amso. Featuring Dave Ananth. sources.title: Why GST and PAYE Must Be Kept Separate
sources.summary: Dave Ananth discusses keeping tax money separate and recognising when unpaid tax points to a deeper business problem.
sources.text: In this discussion Money held for tax should not be confused with the money available to run a business. In this extract from Notes From The Executive, hosted by Mina Amso, Dave Ananth discusses the practical discipline of keeping GST and PAYE separate from operating cash. A bank balance may include amounts that will need to be paid to Inland Revenue rather than spent on rent, suppliers or other commitments. The clip recommends maintaining a separate tax account and transferring an appropriate portion of incoming revenue into it. The appropriate amount depends on the business’s actual tax position and should be established with its accountant. A separate account is a cash-management discipline, not a substitute for correct calculations, returns, payment dates or advice about an existing shortfall. Repeatedly using tax money to keep trading may indicate a deeper cashflow or commercial-viability problem. It can postpone a difficult decision while creating another creditor and further pressure. The useful question is therefore not only how to meet the next IRD payment, but why ordinary business income is failing to cover ordinary business expenses. Dave’s work at Meridian Partners includes student loans, tax disputes and negotiations with Inland Revenue. Where tax debt has already accumulated, accounting information and legal advice can help clarify the situation and the options that may be considered. No separate-account practice or negotiation guarantees that a business will recover or that Inland Revenue will accept a proposal. The underlying commercial problem still needs to be understood and addressed. Practical points Separate tax provisions from day-to-day operating funds. Ask the accountant to establish appropriate amounts and payment obligations. Treat repeated use of tax money as a warning about cashflow. Address the underlying business problem as well as the outstanding tax. Podcast material: Notes From The Executive, hosted by Mina Amso. Featuring Dave Ananth. sources.title: Why Tax Debt Becomes Worse When It Is Ignored
sources.summary: Unresolved tax debt can grow while options narrow. Dave Ananth explains why early engagement matters.
sources.text: In this discussion An unresolved tax balance can become much harder to manage when it is left unattended. In this Notes From The Executive extract, hosted by Mina Amso, Dave Ananth discusses the effect of allowing tax debt to accumulate instead of confronting the underlying problem. The message is about timing and engagement, rather than a particular debt figure. Interest and penalties can increase the amount outstanding while the original liability remains unresolved. If the position continues for years, a once-manageable problem may develop into serious enforcement or an insolvency matter. The amount shown on a statement is only one part of the assessment: business cashflow, ongoing obligations and the stage of Inland Revenue’s response also matter. Business owners should not wait for a statutory demand, liquidation proceeding or final enforcement notice before obtaining accounting and legal advice. Earlier engagement gives advisers an opportunity to establish the facts and consider what information is needed. It does not guarantee that a particular option remains available, that enforcement will pause, or that IRD will reduce the balance. Dave is a Partner at Meridian Partners and works in student loans, tax disputes and negotiations with Inland Revenue. A practical review may require the accountant’s reconstruction of the financial position alongside advice about the tax matter. Sustainable proposals need to reflect what can actually be done, including how current obligations will be met. Inland Revenue retains responsibility for deciding whether any proposed arrangement is acceptable, and past results do not predict the outcome of another case. Practical points Check the liability, interest and penalties rather than ignoring statements. Identify any enforcement notices and response deadlines. Obtain accounting and legal advice before the matter becomes urgent. Base any proposal on realistic finances and ongoing compliance. Podcast material: Notes From The Executive, hosted by Mina Amso. sources.title: When Tax Advice Arrives Too Late
sources.summary: Dave Ananth uses a medical analogy to explain why early advice can preserve options in a developing tax matter.
sources.text: In this discussion By the time a tax matter has become an audit, investigation or prosecution, specialist intervention may resemble emergency surgery. Dave Ananth uses that medical analogy in this extract from Notes From The Executive, hosted by Mina Amso, to explain the difficulty of being asked to help only after a problem has reached a critical stage. The comparison concerns timing. If an unsuitable strategy has already been adopted or proceedings have advanced too far, options that might once have been considered may no longer be available. An adviser needs to understand what has happened, what has been communicated and which decisions or deadlines now shape the matter. A last-minute request cannot undo every earlier step. Early advice can help a person understand the position before committing to a response. It can also clarify where accounting information is needed and which questions require legal consideration. That is different from promising that an investigation or enforcement proceeding can be stopped. Inland Revenue and the courts retain their statutory powers, and the available response depends on the particular facts and law. Dave’s work at Meridian Partners includes student loans, tax disputes and negotiations with Inland Revenue. The clip encourages people to seek appropriate assistance while there is time to assess the situation, rather than waiting for the final notice. Anyone seeking individual advice should begin with a brief enquiry identifying the general issue and any urgent deadline. Detailed confidential information should follow only after conflict checks and formal engagement arrangements are in place. Practical points Seek advice before adopting a response strategy. Keep a clear record of correspondence and steps already taken. Tell the relevant adviser about any deadline at the outset. Do not assume late intervention can reverse proceedings or guarantee an outcome. Podcast material: Notes From The Executive, hosted by Mina Amso. Featuring Dave Ananth. sources.title: Restructuring a Business While Resolving Tax Debt
sources.summary: Two clips from the same anonymised matter show how addressing business viability formed part of a credible tax-debt proposal.
sources.text: In this discussion These two Notes From The Executive clips, hosted by Mina Amso, describe different parts of the same anonymised business-recovery matter. They are presented together because the tax negotiation cannot be understood separately from the underlying commercial changes. Dave Ananth explains that the response involved more than simply asking Inland Revenue to reduce a debt. The business had accumulated substantial tax debt while operating two locations. Its underlying position first needed to be examined. The unviable operation was closed, the financial position was reconstructed with the accountant, available funding was assessed and a credible proposal was then presented to Inland Revenue. Those steps connected the proposed tax response with the business’s capacity to continue. The practical point is that negotiation needs to reflect commercial reality. A proposal is more credible when the business has addressed the cause of its debt and can explain how it expects to meet future obligations. Reliable financial information and an honest assessment of viability are therefore central to the discussion, rather than details to be added after a desired result has been chosen. This is an individual, anonymised example, not an offer of a standard reduction or a repeatable settlement formula. The client’s identity is not disclosed and should not be inferred from the clips. Dave’s work at Meridian Partners includes student loans, tax disputes and negotiations with Inland Revenue. Every matter requires its own assessment; Inland Revenue decides whether to accept a proposal, and the outcome described does not guarantee a similar result for another business. Practical points Read both clips as parts of one anonymised matter. Assess commercial viability before proposing a tax-debt response. Work with the accountant on reliable financial information and funding. Explain how current and future obligations can be met. Do not treat a past outcome as a standard settlement formula.
